issue.title: Home care by neighbourhood, and a care service paid for by the Triple Lock
issue.question: Should the money for a free National Care Service come from changing the Triple Lock on pensions, and who should decide how home care is run?
issue.summary: On 12 November 2026 the government published social care plans. Councils in England are encouraged to commission home care by neighbourhood, with one or two main providers in each, so carers spend their working day in a much smaller area. A study of six providers in Bristol found reorganising visits into zones could deliver the same care with 35% less staff time and 65% less driving. A fully funded National Care Service with free personal care for older people is promised for the next Parliament, and the page says it "will be funded by changes to the triple lock pension". Guidance and toolkits for councils are due in the spring.
issue.slot_reason: Social care had not come up yet in the simulation, and the government's home care plans were in the UK news that day.

news.headline: Government sets out neighbourhood home care plan, National Care Service pledge and £40m GP winter scheme

poll.finding: Told the Prime Minister plans to change the Triple Lock in 2030 and that the money will help fund part of a national care service, 48% supported and 28% opposed. Asked alone, changing the Triple Lock so pensions rise by the higher of inflation or 2.5% got 43% support and 30% oppose. A national care service free at the point of use, funded by government spending, got 74% support and 11% oppose. The poll is about six weeks before the news date, and is the most recent found on this exact question.

bench.title: Fund care by reforming the Triple Lock, with pensioner floor and audit
bench.answer: Keep councils commissioning care, but change the rules. First, the Treasury would publish the Triple Lock change as a costed schedule, with a protected floor so no pensioner's income falls; the poll found 48% support when it funds care (s2). Second, the Department of Health and Social Care would make the neighbourhood-zone guidance (due spring, s1) conditional on carers' fair pay agreement and visit-time minimums, backed by the extra £4.6 billion for councils (s1). Third, an independent auditor reports yearly on visit length, carer travel time and the Bristol-style savings claim of 35% less staff time (s1). It worked if savings reach pay and visit time, and no pensioner loses.

bench.title: Carers and care users co-own each neighbourhood's home care
bench.answer: The government wants one or two main home care providers per neighbourhood, and toolkits for councils are due in spring [s1]. Make the toolkit favour providers owned and run by their own carers and the people they visit, so the neighbourhood team, not a distant head office, sets rotas, visit lengths and pay under the planned fair pay agreement [s1]. Councils would award the neighbourhood contracts on that basis. Study: zoned visits could cut staff time 35% and driving 65% [s1]; let the team keep that saving for pay and longer visits. You would know it worked if the same carers keep turning up, visits are not cut short, and carers stay. Simulated citizens backing familiar local faces: 32 of the panel.

bench.title: Leave pensions alone. Put care users in charge.
bench.answer: Keep the Triple Lock. Fund free personal care for older people from general taxes. The government's neighbourhood care plan offers a starting point [s1]. Councils should fund local care groups owned by the people receiving care and the carers doing it. Give each group an elected board, with care users holding most seats. Pay for full visits and travel time. Put any surplus back into care. Renew funding only when visits happen reliably and people get familiar carers. Publish missed visits, staff pay and time spent with each person every three months. Success means fewer missed visits, familiar faces and carers earning more without rushed care.

gate.verdict: No answer passes every test. B passes the most on how care is run but is silent on money; A and C disagree on whether pensions pay. Who should pay for free care cannot be settled by facts.

jury.question: Should free personal care be paid for by changing the Triple Lock (with a floor for the poorest pensioners), by leaving pensions alone and using general taxes, or should neighbourhood care start first and the money be settled later?
options: Change the Triple Lock to fund care, with a floor for the poorest pensioners
Leave pensions alone and pay for care from general taxes
Start neighbourhood home care now and settle how to pay later
jury.ruling: Leave pensions alone and pay for care from general taxes: the jurors would not take it from older people's income, and wanted the cost spread wider.

reasons.text: Pensioners paid in all their lives. Fund care from general tax, not by shaving what old people live on.
Get the carers sorted first. Same faces each day matters more to me than arguing over pensions.
Pensions rise faster than wages already. A floor for the poorest and a change for the rest seems fair.
Do the local bit now, it is proven. Money fights can wait until we see it working.

minister.trial: In two councils that volunteer, run neighbourhood home care for one year: one main provider per neighbourhood, carers and people receiving care on its board, paid from existing council care budgets. Nothing taken from pensions.
minister.fail_number: Fewer than 6 in 10 visits by one of a person's regular carers, or visits cut short, after 12 months, against each council's own figures today.
minister.statement: Triage. Jury said: hands off pensions, spread the bill wider. Fine. That's a Treasury question. So I'm signing the jury's second choice, not its first: the local bit, on a small patch, from council budgets that already exist. Two councils that volunteer. Same carers, same streets, people who get the care helping steer it. The visit stays a person. If six in ten visits don't come from a regular face in a year, we stop. No national scheme before a pilot that works.
